for_you_if: you enjoy solving mysteries through pure curiosity
you want a game driven entirely by your own discoveries

claims.claim: The game provides minimal initial instruction or guidance, leaving players to figure out flying, landing, and navigation on their own.

citations.review_text: I bought this game because of the hundred thousands positive reviews I saw. Let's start by saying, the games is undoubtebly good, but...It is incredibly confusing, and when I say ''incredibly'' I really mean it. The game doesn't explain you much (basically nothing), ok ok it is design like that and that's ok, but I have to say that sometimes it is pretty irritating too. Flying the space ship is a bit of a headache, you need to get the hang of it. The fact that the loop resets every 22 minutes doesn't make things any easier but you get used to it eventually. With that being said, It is pretty enjoyable. Please note: If you are a person who's short on patience, avoid this game. Trust me!

[h1]Directionless, strange, sometimes even scary.[/h1]
I don't really know what to write, because this is one of those games you don't need to read about.

This game is all about exploring. You don't have any guidance; you just need to go and see everything for yourself. No one will teach you how to land, fly, or avoid obstacles — you learn it all by yourself.

First, I decided to land on the furthest planet from me. Why? Just out of curiosity. Then, I found out that it was actually the scariest planet of them all, and that this game could be genuinely terrifying. There were moments when I wanted to close the game, but then I was like, "Wait a minute... what if I missed something in that one cave?" Curiosity keeps pushing you forward.

Every planet feels different. From gravity to hidden secrets and places you've never seen before. The soundtrack fits every moment perfectly. Sometimes you're just enjoying the scenery, and a few minutes later you're wondering what on Earth is happening.

To sum it up, the less you know about the game before playing it, the better. Trust me on this.

If you don't know anything about Outer Wilds, good. Don't read anything else. Anything else could be a spoiler that would rob you of the single greatest experience ever put to interactive media.
Outer Wilds starts off confusing and directionless. There's some short exposition to tell you the basic premise, a short tutorial to show you the basic elements of navigation, then they give you your ship and say "have fun". Nothing further. If this is the kind of thing that turns you off of a game, you HAVE to push through. Find one weird thing in the world around you or the sky above you and look into it. From there, your list of questions will grow faster than you can answer them.
Then, at the end of the list of questions, you'll have your answers. I don't want to oversell it, but it changes you as a person. Nobody finishes the Outer Wilds as the same person they were when they started the game.

claims.claim: Players must manage survival resources such as fuel and oxygen while exploring planetary environments.

citations.review_text:
Outer Wilds excels in exemplary world design, space travel, and lore, but falls flat in execution, pacing, and gameplay mechanics.

The galaxy is immaculately designed. The soundtrack is befittingly excellent, and the physics have the love and attention to detail you'd expect from a game centered around space exploration. There is clearly an enormous amount of care in how the world is constructed, and uncovering its lore is genuinely rewarding.

Unfortunately, I found that many of the game's core mechanics work against each other.

The survival mechanics, particularly fuel and oxygen management, discourage uninterrupted exploration at your own pace. Instead of being able to settle into an area and explore it naturally, I was frequently thinking about how much time I had left, whether I needed to refuel, or whether I was about to run out of oxygen. The time-loop structure compounds this problem.

It doesn't help that the individual planets aren't always designed with easily distinguishable landmarks in mind. Navigation, both in the ship and on foot, can be extremely cumbersome. The controls and physics eventually become more manageable, but I don't think the game gives you enough breathing room to get comfortable with them before the time constraints start becoming a significant factor.

The puzzles, on the other hand, are one of the game's strongest elements. I found them interesting and challenging, and I appreciated how heavily they rely on the lore and information you uncover throughout the galaxy. Solving a puzzle because you genuinely understood something about the world is a great feeling.

Unfortunately, I often felt like I couldn't think about these puzzles at a comfortable pace. The combination of navigation, environmental hazards, oxygen, fuel, and the time loop created a constant sense of urgency that worked against the kind of deliberate problem-solving the puzzles seemed to encourage.

Ultimately, I felt that the game overstayed its welcome. I was frequ…

This game is one of the greatest video games I've ever experienced. The magic of this game is all in mystery and discovery, and the less you know before starting, the better your first experience will be. So no spoilers in this review. In short, this is an open world mystery taking place inside of a dynamic solar system caught in a time loop. This time loop makes the game feel a bit like a roguelike.

The sense of scale and freedom here isn't compromised like it is in so many other space exploration titles, and yet this solar system isn't procedurally generated with a ton of boring, barren planets either. Everything here is intentionally hand crafted with the game's physics engine in mind. The game's design is for the player's experience rather than realism, which shows in the fact that these planets are a bit small so they can be easily explored properly. So don't expect to spend hours figuring out ship controls or sorting through some cumbersome inventory or crafting system. Flying around does still take some level of skill and learning how physics change with gravity, which feels satisfying when you get the hang of it. When exploring on foot, you do still have to manage things like oxygen and fuel to stay alive in certain atmospheres. This game really found the right balance between being fun and being immersive in the right ways to feel like a proper space adventure.

The time loop mechanic allows the entire solar system to evolve on a large scale as you play so that exploration isn't just about where you go, but also when you get there in the loop. Things change minute to minute in countless ways that you'll have to discover for yourself, but it really brings another dimension to this game that I haven't seen since The Legend of Zelda Majora's Mask.

Ultimately as good as this exploration is and as fun as it is to fly around in the ship, the true enjoyment here is solving the mystery the entire game revolves around. Most of the storytelling here is done through…

claims.claim: Reviewers note that the only element carrying over across resets is the player's accumulated knowledge.

citations.review_text:
High recommendation, this quickly became one of my favorite puzzle games. Everything happening in a loop means the only thing that carries over is knowledge, and you can theoretically beat the game on your very first loop. But the point of the game is figuring out what is happening, and why, bit by bit, over many loops.

Most definitely played best with zero or minimal spoilers. The ingame hint system does a very good job at suggesting connections to the point of rarely feeling truly lost.

I keep thinking about a question that sounds much smaller than it actually is: what if a video game rewarded you with nothing except understanding?

No experience points. No new weapons. No skill tree. Every run of Outer Wilds ends the same way: twenty-two minutes after you wake up, the sun goes supernova and takes the solar system with it. You might die sooner than that — fly into the sun by accident, say — but you'll never get more than those twenty-two minutes. Then you wake up again, and the loop starts over.

At first, this idea feels almost insulting. I've devoted years of my life to learning the grammar of video games. Explore a cave? You'll probably find an upgrade. Beat a boss? Here's a better sword. Reach a new area? Congratulations, you've unlocked somewhere new to explore.

Outer Wilds quietly removes all of that. The only thing that persists between loops is what you've learned. And it turns out that's enough.

What's strange is how completely this changes your relationship with failure. Falling into a black hole isn't failure. Flying into the sun isn't failure. Forgetting your suit and suffocating in space is embarrassing, but it isn't failure either. They're all just ways of learning something you didn't know twenty minutes ago.

There's a moment, maybe five or six hours in, when I realized I wasn't a hero. I was a detective. Every planet is a witness with a fragmented memory. The Nomai ruins scattered across them aren't there to tell a story in order — they're notes left by people who assumed someone else would eventually piece the rest together. Outer Wilds trusts you to be that someone, and because it trusts you, the discoveries feel like yours.

Not because every puzzle is especially hard, though a few are — one or two tipped into tedious enough that I looked up the answer rather than keep circling it. It's that nobody interrupts to explain why any of it matters. I wanted to know because I wanted to know. The universe just keeps existing, indiffer…

You’re basically tossed into space in a ship that looks like a wooden deathtrap, given 22 minutes before the sun blows up, and then... back to square one. No leveling up, no cool gear unlocks, no shiny waypoints telling you where to go. The only thing you carry over when you die is whatever you figured out in your own head during that run.

This is not a horror game, but it's terrifying. 

Nothing is chasing you. Nothing wants to harm you, kill you, or even just scare you. Everything's indifferent to everything. But this also means that if there's no evil, there also is no good. You are on your own, helplessly drifting away while trying to make sense of as much as you can with the little time you have left, before the cold logic of cosmic wilderness wipes you out like a fly on a windshield.

Kinda like life, but with the difference that, here, when you die, you can conveniently carry your knowledge and experience across from your previous life to the next one, so you don't panic again when falling into the black hole at the center of that planet (just looking at it makes me feel uncomfortable) after trying to avoid it for the whole game.
I was legit frightened to look at my screen when it happened, not in fear of losing progress and having to start over, but because it unsettled something so primordial inside me that I really didn't care to react to it. All I wanted was to look away, avert my eyes from the unfolding disaster. In a sense, not wanting to know the outcome of it.
And that is very telling of what cripples you everyday, when facing decisions, as your willingness to take action is suffocated by the absurd weight of your fears and paranoias possibly taking shape and freezing you, much like you freeze in outer space.

But staying still gets you nowhere, and moving (even towards the event horizon) gets you everywhere. Once you realize there's no singularity at the end of the black hole (f*** you general relativity) and you just pop out of some other hole, you honestly feel embarrassed at how you freaked out expecting the end of the world. Just like there's no singularity at the end of your public speaking, or after answering a call from an unknown number, or even after asking the girl you like out for dinner.
And in this game, you have to completely rely on the same failsafe mechanism hardwired …

So far I recommend getting this game on a sale. My reasons are below: 

1. The story is fantastic. I love a game that allows me to find out the story through notes and random notes I can find if done in a good manner. The Outer Wilds gives enough information to make the player curious
2. Flying and Ship controls are Janky fun - you'll be doing a lot of flying and jetpacking around terrain. A good jetpack and ship are a must!...Thankfully it doesn't matter too much if you crash 
3. Unique and memorable: there isn't another game really like this one. You'll see in a lot of these really weird, vague reviews that you HAVE TO play the game to understand...but really that's a lie.  Honestly this game is basically a walking simulator with a few very small puzzles inbetween. Don't play this game expecting a lot of interactivity as the fate of your time has already been set. 

Why I recommend on a SALE not full price: 

1. The game can be boring/tedious - Without too much knowledge of how the game runs or how the story moved forward, there is no really good way of determining your next step which can be annoying for some players. You have a journal/computer that tracks what you find but some clues on one planet lead to another and vice versa so you'll have a ton of open "side quests" to check into. Then if you get the timing wrong for some things (timing of when you do events is SUPER important) you need to restart the run/loop
2. It's a walking simulator - I'm not too big of games that don't provide interactivity. If I wanted that, I would watch a movie. There really is NOT much to do in this game other than run, fly, and read a note. You can find some tech that you can interact with for about a minute or two but most of your time playing the game will be flying, trying to piece together random lore, and note taking.
3. There is no good ending - This allows you to find all previous actions taken to show the player how they got to this point...But it never lets the player ch…
Yes the narrative is beautiful but I don't feel the frustration I experienced in the playthrough (and the god awful flight controls) was worth it for that ending

[h2]The Masterpiece of Exploration (Positives)[/h2]
The story and world-building in Outer Wilds are incredibly good. Even though I played using a keyboard, the controls very responsive and had no issues navigating the environments. The central gameplay mechanic [spoiler]the time loop that resets every 22 minutes[/spoiler] gives the experience a truly unique feeling. I still remember my first time entering Dark Bramble on a friend's recommendation, it was an "unforgettable" experience (yeah...). For players who love exploration driven by a mysterious premise and don't mind a bit of horror, this is one of the best games out there.

[h2]The Friction of Discovery (Negatives)[/h2]
The game features a non-linear world, which is part of its charm, but it can be a double-edged sword. Personally, I found that combining non-linear exploration with very linear, specific puzzles wasn't quite my cup of tea. My personal approach was to "randomly walk" and explore all the planets first, then use the ship’s rumor log to try and solve the puzzles, but I eventually felt a sense of frustration. While the game presents a sense of total freedom, the puzzles actually have very specific answers scattered across a vast map. This makes the "freedom" feel arbitrary, as you are often just hunting for one specific clue to progress.

[h2]Final Verdict[/h2]
My first six hours were a blast, starting with my character dying in the first two minutes because I tried to jump into a geyser on Timber Hearth (my bad). However, after that initial magic wore off, the experience became a bit painful. If you enjoy the "needle in a haystack" style of puzzle-solving where you must find one specific hint in a massive world, you will love this. But for me, the transition from discovery to hunting for specific solutions eventually became more irritating than fun.

cohorts.label: 20-100h
cohorts.summary: Deeper exploration reveals physics-based space movement, knowledge-based progression, and challenging puzzles alongside solid performance.

claims.claim: Reviewers note that the game features true-to-physics movement in space where objects in motion continue moving until hitting an obstacle, which can make controls challenging at first.

citations.review_text:
I agree with the vast number of reviews that have already been written about how excellent the story of this game is, and how fun it is to explore for yourself and progress through the game solely with your own knowledge--no levelling up or collecting items to help you, the only thing unlocking new areas is the fact that you've learned how to get to them. The aesthetics are also beautiful (and will run on even a semi-bad computer, I have a nice computer now but originally played it on a computer with an Intel i7, if you turn down the graphics all the way it will hopefully run and not otherwise impede your playing) and the music is lovely (and plot relevant!). After playing this game, nearly all of my searching for games on Steam has somewhat been "what would be like Outer Wilds??" (even though there really seems to be nothing quite like it). 

I will say that there are some aspects of the game that may not make it the right game for everyone, while the basegame is not intentionally scary you do find yourself frequently faced with the vastness and danger of space, and some people won't like that. Additionally, the controls are true-to-physics in a way that many people find challenging at first. Specifically, if you are actually in space and accelerate, you will literally never slow down unless you purposely fire your rockets going the other way. An object in motion in this game does actually stay in motion until it hits something (which uhh.. warning. you will hit things. many times). Lots of video games add imaginary friction to space, this one does not. 

You also have to learn to embrace dying and mistakes. You will likely mess up many, many, many times over the course of a playthrough of this game. Personally, I actually found that this game helped me to relax a little bit more about dying in video games -- the consequences are never permanent, so all you have to do is start again, but it can be frustrating at times. Luckily, it is an open-world, nonlinear game, …

Had a blast!

HOWEVER!!!!!!!!!!

What I'd recommend to people before playing is if you have a decent PC there are some secret settings you need to adjust to increase your fps. I spent the first 30 mins in the starting area wondering why my game felt so slow. The file is secretsettings.txt and it's found in the appdata folder.

Next up, I turned off autopilot from the get go. I learned the ship controls from scratch and HAD SO MUCH FUN! It was thrilling to fly about the system manually, had quite a few close calls that had me on the edge of my seat!

Without spoiling much I do have an issue with the puzzels. I love games that have harder puzzels, ones that leave me thinking for ages, banging my head against the wall, sleeping it off, until the solution sparks in my mind. There were moments in this game that had that which felt great! But there would've been many more moments like that if there had been less lore text that just gives you the answer. 

I noticed many little ingenuious clues to various puzzels, but I only noticed them after the lore text gave away the answer. Without the lore text, the puzzels would've been way harder and therefore would've been less appealing to the general public. However I would've greatly appreciated a harder difficulty where the lore text didn't give so much away.

Overall I don't think game has left a large lasting impact on me compared to other reviewers. But I did have lot's of fun.

Personally, I actually found that this game helped me to relax a little bit more about dying in video games -- the consequences are never permanent, so all you have to do is start again, but it can be frustrating at times. Luckily, it is an open-world, nonlinear game, …
Perhaps the most impressive achievement of this game is that it runs so well on my poor hardware! A real masterpiece.

For a long time, I didn't think I’d see another game that would instantly rank among my all-time favorites, nor did I expect to encounter anything truly surprising outside of tech demos. That was until Outer Wilds opened my eyes

I won’t go into too much detail, as the originality behind the concept is precisely what makes it so exceptional. It is a unique experience in every regard—from its design and technical execution to its story. Truly, it is a must-play title and, without a doubt, a rare kind of surprise. For me, it is one of those games you simply have to experience at least once in your life

That said, I do understand the criticisms leveled at the DLC. It can create pacing issues and bottlenecks not found in the base game—particularly one very tough section where, unless you discover, understand, or investigate something very specific, you end up going in circles. Even so, I don’t think I’ve ever felt as much anxiety in a game as I did in Echoes of the Eye. The feeling of being small against the vastness of my surroundings really resonates with me, and it was something I discovered while playing this DLC. It is amazing how it flips the base formula on its head while using the same mechanics, thereby enriching the story as well. It isn't for everyone, but it is certainly worth trying so you can discover it for yourself

[b]An instant classic[/b]

To be honest I bounced off this game at first because I didn't find it particularly exciting, visually appealing, or interesting as reading random logs was fatiguing and didn't mean anything. But I pushed through again, going to a different planet, and was hooked.

This game was one of the most satisfying gaming experiences I've ever had and I hope whoever reads this also gives it a try. If you don't like it at first, like I did, try being a bit for brave and adventurous. There is so much packed into this small solar system. This game is one of the few you really need to play blind as learning and knowledge are everything.

The DLC is VERY obtuse and not as easy to understand as the base game. I wouldn't consider it mandatory, but it fills in some of the gaps and introduces some cool mechanics. Try the base game and get the DLC if you really want more.

A fantastic puzzle game with a focus on exploration and learning about the world. Really, there's not much I can critique about the main game - it's one of the best in the genres in my opinion. The expansion, Echoes of the Eye, is also very good though I did struggle with motivation more on that one. It all pays off with a great puzzle of it's own, but wandering around and failing to execute a plan effectively feels more like a waste of time than in the main game. I played probably 35 hours of this game, and 15 of that was Echoes of the Eye because of the backtracking and making multiple "runs" for the same objective. Still good, not as great as the main game.

claims.claim: Reviewers mention that the game does not use traditional equipment or level-gating for progression, relying entirely on player knowledge to access new areas.

citations.review_text:
One of the greatest puzzle games of all time.

You're given freedom to explore the solar system from the very start and it's up to you to piece the clues together on how to finish the game.

Little by little you understand more about how everything works and how different planets link together. This game is full of unique mechanics.

Each planet has it's own characteristics and challenges to overcome, but you can approach them in any order you like. Nothing is gated, there is no "late game" equipment. All you need is time and knowledge to figure it out.

Masterpiece.

I agree with the vast number of reviews that have already been written about how excellent the story of this game is, and how fun it is to explore for yourself and progress through the game solely with your own knowledge--no levelling up or collecting items to help you, the only thing unlocking new areas is the fact that you've learned how to get to them. The aesthetics are also beautiful (and will run on even a semi-bad computer, I have a nice computer now but originally played it on a computer with an Intel i7, if you turn down the graphics all the way it will hopefully run and not otherwise impede your playing) and the music is lovely (and plot relevant!). After playing this game, nearly all of my searching for games on Steam has somewhat been "what would be like Outer Wilds??" (even though there really seems to be nothing quite like it). 

I will say that there are some aspects of the game that may not make it the right game for everyone, while the basegame is not intentionally scary you do find yourself frequently faced with the vastness and danger of space, and some people won't like that. Additionally, the controls are true-to-physics in a way that many people find challenging at first. Specifically, if you are actually in space and accelerate, you will literally never slow down unless you purposely fire your rockets going the other way. An object in motion in this game does actually stay in motion until it hits something (which uhh.. warning. you will hit things. many times). Lots of video games add imaginary friction to space, this one does not. 

You also have to learn to embrace dying and mistakes. You will likely mess up many, many, many times over the course of a playthrough of this game. Personally, I actually found that this game helped me to relax a little bit more about dying in video games -- the consequences are never permanent, so all you have to do is start again, but it can be frustrating at times. Luckily, it is an open-world, nonlinear game, …

Outer wilds just captures your attention from the start till the credits roll, and there is no dull moment. It is kind of game that when credits roll, you're just stunned that what you just played and you feel hollow that it has ended. It is like a journey which you never want to end.  One of the rare occasions where mystery element is done right in games. This game gives you freedom in every way, exploration is open ended and never gatekeeps you from getting creative with it, only limitation is your knowledge. First blind playthrough of this game is something special, so don't spoil it by looking up stuff about this game, even the minor details can fade the fun experience. It rewards curiosity, exploration and how you use your tools. Really great game and I wholeheartedly recommend it.

claims.claim: Reviewers report that the game lacks objective markers and hand-holding, relying instead on player curiosity and a ship's log to track progress through knowledge rather than leveling up.

citations.review_text:
There are games that entertain you, games that challenge you, and games that stay with you long after you've finished them. Outer Wilds belongs firmly in the last category. It isn't simply one of the best games I've ever played—it is one of the most memorable experiences I've had in any form of storytelling.

From the moment you take your first flight, the game fills you with an overwhelming sense of curiosity. It never holds your hand, never points you toward a checklist of objectives, and never tells you exactly where to go. Instead, it trusts you to explore. Every strange landmark, every mysterious ruin, and every celestial body invites a single question: "What's going on here?"

The brilliance of Outer Wilds lies in its design. Progress isn't measured by leveling up or collecting better equipment. Your only real reward is knowledge. Every discovery naturally leads to another question, and every answer makes the universe feel larger, richer, and more interconnected than before. Few games respect the player's intelligence as much as this one does.

The solar system feels alive in a way that's difficult to describe. Every planet has its own personality, its own rules, and its own unforgettable sights. Exploring them is consistently exciting because you never know what you'll find next. The game rewards observation, experimentation, and simple curiosity more than almost anything else.

Its soundtrack deserves special praise as well. The music is beautiful, comforting, mysterious, and emotional all at once. There are moments where a single melody, paired with what you're seeing, creates an atmosphere that words struggle to capture.

What makes Outer Wilds truly exceptional, however, is that it can only be experienced for the first time once. It's a game built entirely around discovery. Once you understand its mysteries, you can never truly play it as a newcomer again. That makes every revelation feel precious, and it makes recommending the game surprisingly difficult…

[spoiler-free review]
What an amazing game. What a unique, captivating experience.

If you're considering buying this game: it's great, but it's not a game for everyone. If you're looking for a high action game with combat, with quest markers telling you where to go, where you can unlock new abilities and grow more powerful over time: this is not it. The action here consists of walking and flying around, and a lot of reading. The only thing guiding you is your curiosity. The only progression happens in your head, while you slowly learn more about the world and its previous inhabitants.

This is a game for curious people, and - dare I say it - intelligent, slightly nerdy people. People who think archaeology and astrophysics are fascinating instead of boring and stuffy. This game lets you be an archaeologist and astronaut without all the boring bits: visit unique and beautiful places and learn about lost civilizations without all the waiting and digging.

One important thing: you can only truly experience this knowledge-based game once, so: don't look up any tips; don't look up anything about this game while you're playing. It's very easy to get spoilers which destroy the experience. If you think you're stuck: just read your ship's log again and sleep on it. If you're still really stuck: go to the subreddit, where they're good at giving personalized tips without spoilers.
